```{.quiz-yaml}
id: 15_related_anova_third_condition
title: What does the third condition add?
questions:
  - id: which_is_practice
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      Which comparison gives the best indication of any improvement due to
      practice, as opposed to social facilitation?
    options:
      - text: First alone vs. second alone
        correct: true
      - text: First alone vs. competition
      - text: Second alone vs. competition
    explanation: >
      Both solo trials happen before any competition, so they show how much
      the children improved without a rival. Other changes between trials,
      such as fatigue, could matter too. First alone vs. competition is the
      comparison Chapter 13 made, and it mixes practice with the introduction
      of a competitor.

  - id: competition_and_order
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      All five children competed on their third trial. What makes it hard to
      attribute their improvement from the second trial to social facilitation?
    options:
      - text: They had another trial of practice as well as a competitor
        correct: true
      - text: Different children contributed scores to the two conditions
      - text: Their stable differences in speed only appeared on the third trial
    explanation: >
      Competition always comes later, so further practice could explain some
      or all of that improvement. Using the same children removes stable
      differences in overall speed from the comparison, but it doesn't remove
      changes that happen between trials. Counterbalancing the later trials
      would help, as we discussed in Chapter 13.

  - id: no_single_difference
    type: multiple-choice
    prompt: >
      In Chapter 13 we dealt with the differences between children by
      subtracting: each child's two times became one difference score, and we
      tested those. What's the problem with doing that here?
    options:
      - text: No single pairwise difference covers all three conditions
        correct: true
      - text: Subtracting would take out the differences between conditions too
      - text: With the same children in every condition, there are no differences between children to remove
    explanation: >
      With three conditions there are three pairs, so each child has three
      differences. We could test each one, but that brings back Chapter 14's
      problem of making several comparisons. Subtracting wasn't the issue:
      it keeps the differences between conditions, which is why it worked in
      Chapter 13. And the differences between children haven't gone anywhere.
      Using the same children keeps them out of the comparison between
      conditions, but some children are still faster than others in every
      condition. So we need another way of setting those differences aside.
```
